title: Toldot: two nations (Genesis 25:23)
hook: two peoples in one womb; commentators read Jacob and Esau as two ways of being

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebekah's blunt question, lamah zeh anochi. Your line was why am I thus. Today, she gets an answer.

Some mornings pull two ways at once. Go for a run, fix the fence, get something done. Or stay in with a book and a cup of tea and think. One person can hold both, and they argue. Rebekah, in pain, has gone to ask God why her twins are fighting inside her. The answer she gets is bigger than a pregnancy: two whole peoples, two whole ways of living, already pushing against each other before they've taken a breath.
screen: `THE PART THAT WANTS TO RUN.` → `THE PART THAT WANTS TO STAY IN.` → `REBEKAH GETS HER ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The answer, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, begins: "Two nations are in thy womb." Two peoples will separate from within you; one will be stronger than the other, and the elder will serve the younger. Some readers note the Hebrew of that last line is compact enough that it could even be read the other way around. The twins are born. The first comes out red and hairy all over, like a cloak, and they call him Esau. The second comes out holding his brother's heel, akev in Hebrew, and they call him Jacob, Ya'akov. Then the Torah draws two portraits in one verse. Esau becomes a skillful hunter, a man of the field. Jacob is an ish tam, a word that means whole, or simple, or quiet, and he dwells in tents. And the parents split. Isaac loves Esau, because he likes the game Esau hunts. Rebekah loves Jacob. Some readers take the brothers as two ways of being in the world: the field and the tent, action and reflection, appetite and patience, the hunter who lives in the moment and the one who stays home and thinks about tomorrow. A midrash, retold by Rashi, even has the two struggling in the womb over which way to go. Rashi and the midrash often read Esau harshly. The plain text is more mixed. In the coming days, Jacob takes things that aren't simply his, and Esau cries a great and bitter cry. Two nations in one womb. And maybe, some readers say, two nations in one person.
screen: `TWO NATIONS ARE IN THY WOMB.` · `RED ESAU, JACOB AT THE HEEL.` · `THE FIELD AND THE TENT.` · `TWO WAYS OF BEING.` · then, large: `TWO IN ONE WOMB.`

segments.voice: Find your Esau, the part of you that wants to act, to grab, to be out in the field right now, and say hello to it without judging. Then find your Jacob, the part that wants to wait, to plan, to stay in the tent, and say hello to that one too. Notice which one has been in charge lately, and let both sit here, for once, in one body.
Toldot. Generations: the portion where twins struggle in one womb, and are born as two different ways of living.
Your line: two in one womb. The field and the tent, side by side. Day one hundred eighty-seven in the books.

howItsDone: Toldot is read in synagogues each late autumn, and Jewish teachers often use Jacob and Esau to talk about the different drives inside one person and within one family.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording 'Two nations are in thy womb' (Genesis 25:23).
'The Hebrew could be read the other way around' (rav ya'avod tza'ir, without a direct-object marker) is a known observation; confirm framing.
The midrash of the twins struggling in the womb (Jacob toward houses of study, Esau toward idol temples) is only alluded to; Genesis Rabbah 63:6 and Rashi on 25:22. Confirm.
'Commentators read Jacob and Esau as two ways of being' is a general statement from the index; a Keeper may want a named commentator.
Rabbinic tradition also reads Esau as Edom and later Rome; not included here by design.
